segments.text: Introduction. History is not an accident. When the book of Daniel opens, the world appears broken.
In 605 BC, Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem and marches royal youth into exile. Sacred
vessels from the Temple of Yahweh are deposited into the house of the god Marduk in Babylon,
KJV Daniel 1-2. To the casual observer, the god of Israel has been defeated by imperial might.
Yet, Daniel 1-2 immediately upends that view. And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah
into his hand. Daniel 1-2. KJV. Human tyrants do not direct history independently. Nebuchadnezzar
did not conquer Jerusalem by his own strength. God handed it over according to his prophetic purpose.
Earthly empires rise and fall under God's rule. Daniel 4-17. Prophecy is revealed to
the prophets. Amos 3-7. It is God's historical roadmap, demonstrating his sovereignty over
every superpower and pointing forward to the redemptive arrival of Jesus Christ.
Part 1. Three ways to read the prophecies. How you read decides what you see. Before you
try to name a single beast, horn, or date, you make a choice about how to read. That choice is
your hermeneutics, simply the method and rules you use to interpret scripture.
Daniel and Revelation are full of symbols, such as beasts, horns, and metals,
and they speak about things to come. For centuries, Christians have read them in three
main ways. Each way answers one question. When do these prophecies happen?
Historicism says, all along, in one unbroken line from Daniel's day to Christ's return.
Preterism says, back then, in the past. Futurism says, mostly later, at the very end.
This course follows the first. A fourth way, idealism, treats the visions as pictures of
the timeless fight between good and evil instead of events in history, so this course leaves it
aside. The choice matters because it decides what you will see in every chapter that follows.
1. Historicism, the continuous historical model
Historicism reads Daniel and Revelation as an unbroken, contiguous chain of fulfillment
extending from the prophet's day through the rise and fall of world empires across the Christian
era and straight to the Second Coming. In plain words, the prophecies are fulfilled all along,
one after another, in one line that never breaks, from Daniel's own time to Christ's return.
Who held it? Hippolytus of Rome, about AD 200, listed Babylon, Persia, Greece,
and Rome as four kingdoms in one sequence. That list is the chain this course follows.
Hippolytus also expected one future Antichrist. That is a different idea,
and the Futurism card below describes it. Later, John Wycliffe and the main Protestant reformers,
Martin Luther, John Calvin, Philip Melanchthon, John Knox, read the chain through the whole
Christian era, and so did Sir Isaac Newton. Why it works
It obeys the explicit text of Daniel 2.38-44 and adds nothing to it. Three things follow from that.
It has no unbiblical gaps. The passage gives an order and never breaks it.
Daniel 2.38 says, thou art this head of gold. Daniel 2.39 says, after thee shall arise another
kingdom inferior to thee, and another third kingdom of brass. Daniel 2.40 says, the fourth
kingdom shall be strong as iron. Each kingdom comes after the one before it. The passage
never pauses, skips the Christian centuries, or starts again later, and this reading adds
no waiting period that the verses do not print. It is continuous all the way to the Second Coming.
After the legs of iron come the divided feet. Then, in Daniel 2.44,
God sets up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed. In this reading,
that kingdom arrives at the Second Coming, the stone that fills the earth.
The Christian centuries are not skipped. They are covered by the legs of iron and the divided
feet, so the line runs without a break from the head of gold to Christ's return.
It is coherent. It makes sense. Each part leads into the next, so the whole fits together as one
story. At any point, you can say where you are on the line, what came before, and what comes next,
and you never need a missing piece to make it work. In short, nothing is missing, nothing is
added, and the line never breaks. 2. Preterism. Confined to the past.
Preterism says the prophecies were fulfilled in the past, soon after they were written.
The word comes from a Latin word meaning past. In plain words, the book is about then, not about
the ages that come after. Two different readings end the story in the past, and they are not
the same reading. 3. The reading of Daniel. It says the prophecies end in the second century BC,
when the Greek-Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes attacked the Jews and defiled their temple.
This is often called the Maccabean reading, after the Maccabees, the Jewish family who led the
revolt. An ancient critic named Porphyry argued for it. It ends the story centuries before the
cross, so Rome and the divided kingdoms never arrive. 4. The reading of Revelation.
The Spanish Jesuit scholar Luis de Alcazar first set this out in a full book in 1614. He read
Revelation 1-11 as the fall of Jerusalem and the rest as the overthrow of pagan Rome.
The Christian centuries fall off the end of the story here too. Why people hold it?
It ties each prophecy to events that anyone can look up in history,
and it lets the book speak to the people who first read it. Why it does not fit the text.
Daniel does not stop where this reading stops. There are three reasons,
and later sittings test each one in full. The statue keeps going. Daniel 8-20-21
names Media and Persia together as one kingdom, and then Greece. That makes Greece the bronze,
the third metal. In Daniel 2, the bronze is followed by legs of iron, then feet of iron
and clay, and only then does the stone strike. Daniel 2 33-35. Antiochus ruled one piece of the
Greek kingdom, so a story that ends with him leaves the legs, the feet, and the stone with nowhere to
go. God's kingdom never ends. Daniel 2 44 says the kingdom God sets up shall never be destroyed
and shall stand forever. No kingdom from the second century BC did that. The Jewish state that
came out of the Maccabean Revolt ended under Rome, which took Judea in 63 BC.
Gabriel points to the end. He tells Daniel that, at the time of the end shall be the vision.
Daniel 8-17. Antiochus died in 164 BC, long before any end. What it costs.
The ages after Antiochus, and after Rome, drop off the line. Believers who live in those ages
are left with no prophecy to show them where they stand.
3. Futurism. Postponed to the end of time. Futurism says the last part of Daniel's
prophecy, and most of Revelation, belongs to the future. It agrees that the kingdoms ran
in order as far as Rome. Then it says the prophetic clock stopped. Many centuries pass
with nothing in the prophecy, and the clock starts again shortly before Christ returns,
for one short final crisis under a single ruler, the Antichrist. That long pause is the gap.
The week said to be paused is the 70th week of Daniel 9.
Roberta's own figure for the final crisis was three and a half years. A later dispensational
reading stretches it into a literal seven-year week. Origins. Some early Christian writers,
such as Hippolytus of Rome, about AD 200, already expected one future Antichrist.
About 1590, the Spanish Jesuit Francisco Rivera turned that expectation into a full reading,
with a gap before a future crisis. In Protestant circles, SR Maitland took it up,
and Edward Irving and John Nelson Darby then spread it. That gave rise to modern dispensationalism,
later spread by the Schofield Reference Bible. Why people hold it. Many Christians expect a final
crisis before Christ returns, and the Bible does speak of one, Daniel 12.1. A short crisis in the
future is also easy to picture. Why it does not fit the text. The final crisis is not the problem.
The problem is the long pause futurism puts before it, because no verse prints that pause.
The statue has no pause in it. In Daniel 2, the legs of iron run straight into the feet of iron
and clay. Daniel 2.41 says of the feet, the kingdom shall be divided, but there shall be in
it of the strength of the iron. It is the same fourth kingdom, divided but still strong,
not a new one that appears after a long wait. The stone then strikes the feet, Daniel 2.34.
The 70 weeks have no pause in them. Daniel 9.24 says 70 weeks are determined,
upon Daniel's people, as one block of time. Nothing in verses 24-27 says the clock stops
after the 69th week. The gap is added from outside the verse, and it moves the 70th week
about 2,000 years away from the other 69. The pause leaves out the ages we live in.
The line jumps from Rome to the end of the world, so no prophecy tells believers where they stand
today. What it costs. The whole Christian age drops off the line, and the 70th week,
which this course reads as the week of Christ's cross, is moved away from Christ.
Sitting 9 shows why that week belongs to the Messiah.
The historical catalyst, Council of Trent, Preterism and Futurism, as full systems,
did not appear out of nowhere. In the 1500s, the Protestant reformers read Daniel and Revelation
as one line running through the Christian centuries. On that line, they found the medieval
papal system in the place the prophecies give to the little horn of Daniel 7 and the beast of
Revelation 13. The power that comes after the kingdoms speaks against God and wears out the
saints. The Catholic Church answered the Reformation at the Council of Trent,
1545-1563, and Jesuit scholars then published two full alternatives.
Rivera, about 1590, placed the fulfillment in a distant future, and Alcazar, 1614,
placed it in the pagan past. Others had read prophecy these ways before them,
but these were the first complete systems set against historicism. In plain words,
each one takes the Christian centuries and the power the reformers named in them off the line.
The book titles and publication dates are on record, so you can check this claim yourself.
Interpretation
The bottom line. The three readings answer one question. When do the prophecies happen?
Historicism says all along, in one unbroken line from Babylon to Christ's kingdom.
Preterism says back then, so it ends the story too soon. Futurism says mostly later,
so it cuts the line in the middle with a gap that no verse names.
Only historicism keeps every part of the text where the text puts it.
Here is why that matters enough to spend a whole sitting on it.
Everything that follows in this course reads Daniel one way or the other.
If the prophecies ended with Antiochus, then the chapters that come after Greece
describe nothing, and the Christian centuries have no place on the map.
If they pause for a gap and resume at the end, then the same centuries have no place either,
and the book has nothing to say about the age you actually live in.
Either way, you are left reading a map that stops before your own house.
Historicism is the reading that does not ask you to add anything.
The chapter gives an order and never breaks it.
Thou art this head of gold, then another kingdom, after thee, then a third, then a fourth,
and then the kingdom God sets up. Daniel 2 38 to 44.
You start at the head that is named, walk forward, and arrive where the text arrives.
No waiting period is inserted, and no century is skipped.
So the bottom line is also a test you can apply yourself.
When you meet a claim about Daniel, ask it one question.
Does this keep every part of the text where the text puts it,
or does it have to move something to make the pieces fit?
A reading that has to move the cross, the divided kingdoms,
or your own age out of the way is not being careful with the passage.
The reading this course follows is the one that leaves everything where Daniel put it
and finds Christ at the end of it.
We have come to the first checkpoint.
Part 2 The Year Day Scale
The Year Day Principle
Prophecy that speaks in symbols, these visions are called apocalyptic,
measures time in symbols too.
In Daniel 7 the four beasts are four kings, Daniel 7 17.
The fourth beast is called a kingdom, Daniel 7 23,
and the ten horns are ten kings, Daniel 7 24.
If the beasts and horns are symbols, the time given beside them is part of the symbol.
The historicist reading counts a prophetic day as one year of real history.
Here is why.
Scripture itself uses a day for a year, twice, before Daniel does.
Scripture defines its own prophetic time scale.
The Torah Foundation Numbers 14 34
When Israel rebelled after the spies had spent 40 days in Canaan,
God set a punishment of one year for each day.
Each day for a year shall ye bear your iniquities, even 40 years.
The Exile Foundation Ezekiel 4 6
The prophet Ezekiel lived among the exiles in Babylon.
Ezekiel 1 2 dates his call to the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity.
He was commanded to lie on his side as a sign of Jerusalem's coming siege,
and God told him, I have appointed thee each day for a year.
Ezekiel 4 6
Each day he lay there stood for one year.
The Self-Checking Anchor Daniel 9 24-27
In Daniel 9, the angel Gabriel assigns 70 weeks upon thy people and upon thy holy city
to finish transgression, make reconciliation for iniquity, and anoint the Most Holy.
A week is seven, so 70 weeks is 70 x 7 equals 490 days.
490 literal days are barely 16 months, far too short a span in which to rebuild Jerusalem,
re-establish the nation, and see the Messiah minister and die.
Only when those 70 weeks are read as 490 years does the prophecy run from the Persian Decree
to restore Jerusalem to the public ministry of Jesus Christ and his cross,
with the week then closing.
In this reading, those points are 457 B.C., Artaxerxes Decree, Ezra 7,
A.D. 27, his baptism, A.D. 31, the cross, and A.D. 34, the close of the week.
A later sitting walks the edition that joins them.
Once Daniel 9 has tested the year day principle,
the longer prophetic spans rest on the same measuring rod.
Daniel 7.25 says, A time and times and the dividing of time.
A time is one year, times are two, and the dividing of a time is half a year,
three and a half years.
Revelation writes that same span as 1,260 days, Revelation 12.6.
Daniel 8.14 says 2,300 days.
On this scale, those days are years.
This sitting names the counts.
Later sittings say what history they cover.
An honest reading, Numbers 14.34 and Ezekiel 4.6
set the scale where God appoints it.
One prophetic day for one year.
Daniel 9 applies it.
490 literal days cannot rebuild Jerusalem and reach Messiah,
so the 70 weeks, 490 years, run from Artaxerxes seventh year decree,
457 B.C., Ezra 7, to Messiah's baptism, A.D. 27, and his cross in A.D. 31,
with the week closing in A.D. 34.
The appointment belongs to symbolic time,
the kind of vision in which a beast is a kingdom and the days are part of the symbol.
It does not travel into every prophecy that mentions a day.
Daniel lived the 10 days of pulse, Daniel 1.12-15,
the three years of his training, Daniel 1.5,
and the three full weeks of his mourning, Daniel 10.2-3.
Jonah's 40 days were a warning Nineveh could still answer, Jonah 3.4.
In the days of these kings, Daniel 2.44, names an era,
and a later sitting will show that Daniel 4's seven times
pass over one king and end in his own lifetime.
Second Peter 3.8 speaks of God's patience.
One day with the Lord as a thousand years and is a different saying.
Where the vision is already a symbol and a literal count cannot carry what it claims,
the day stands for a year.
Where the text is a life someone lived, a day remains a day.
We have come to the second checkpoint.
Part 3. The Centrality of Jesus Christ
The redemptive core of prophecy.
Prophetic interpretation must never become a cold intellectual exercise
or a tool for political fear-mongering.
The unbroken historicist chain exists for one primary purpose,
to exalt Jesus Christ as the Lord of human history and our personal redeemer.
One. Jesus in Daniel 1, the sovereign hand.
The exile appeared to be the death of the covenant,
but Daniel 1.2 shows that the same God who later gave his son on Calvary
was already governing the fall of Judah.
God orchestrates trials not to abandon his people,
but to purge them of idolatry and prepare the global stage for the Messiah's advent.
Two. Jesus in Daniel 9, the slain sacrifice.
The pinnacle of Daniel's prophetic timeline is not an earthly empire
or a future political tyrant, it is the cross.
Daniel 9.26 announces that Messiah will be cut off, but not for himself.
Daniel 9.27 then says that he will confirm the covenant
and in the middle of the week cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease.
This reading takes he to be that same Messiah, and sitting 9 gives the reasons.
By offering his own sinless blood on Calvary, Jesus fulfilled the entire sacrificial system,
ending the need for animal offerings forever.
Three. Jesus in Daniel 2, the returning king.
The historicist sequence does not end with Rome,
nor does it stall in the divided kingdoms of Europe, the feet of iron and clay.
It culminates in a supernatural stone cut out without hands,
which smote the image upon his feet, Daniel 2.34,
and became a great mountain that filled the whole earth, Daniel 2.35.
Daniel 2.45 says the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands.
Daniel 2.44 says the God of heaven sets up a kingdom that shall stand forever.
This stone is Jesus Christ, returning in power and glory to inaugurate that everlasting kingdom.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets,
he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Luke 24.27, KJV.
Christ. Every empire on the chain serves the story of the Messiah cut off for us,
Daniel 9, and the king who fills the earth, Daniel 2.44-45.
Prophecy without Christ at the center is a map with no destination.
We have come to the third checkpoint.
Part 4. Why Historicism Matters Today
Look at what the other two readings do to your own time.
If Daniel's prophecies ended in the days of Antiochus IV,
Preterism, the Christian age is not on the line.
If the prophecy skips the Christian centuries and places a future seven-year time of great
trouble after them, later dispensationalism, those centuries are not on the line either.
In both cases, the ages you live in have no map.
Historicism is the one reading that keeps them on the line.
Historicism provides believers with clarity and reassurance.
You know where you stand. You live in the final segment of human history,
the divided nations, the feet of iron and clay, right before the striking of the supernatural
stone. You are freed from fear.
Present superpowers, global crises, and shifting alliances do not dictate the future.
The same God who governed Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome holds today's events in his hands.
You rest in Christ's triumph.
Prophecy proves God's absolute reliability. The same prophetic timeline that precisely
predicted Christ's first advent to bear our sins guarantees his second advent to reign as king.
Before you accept a prophetic conclusion text, does Daniel's succession language,
after thee, support it? History.
Does the chain stay continuous, or does it break into past-only or future-only voids?
Interpretation. Is the year-day scale anchored at the cross in Daniel 9?
Christ. Does this lead you to the Messiah cut off for us and the stone king who fills the earth?
Christology. The unbroken chain exists to exalt Jesus Christ.
The historicist chain is not a political chart.
It exists to exalt Jesus Christ as Lord of history and personal redeemer.
In Daniel 1-2, the same God who gave his son on Calvary already governed Judah's fall.
In Daniel 9-26, Messiah is cut off, but not for himself. The pinnacle of the timeline is the
cross, not an earthly tyrant. In Daniel 2-34-35 and 2-45, the stone cut without hands is Christ
returning to fill the earth. Daniel 2-44 is the everlasting kingdom that shall stand forever.
On the road to Emmaus, Jesus expounded in all the scriptures the things concerning himself,
Luke 24-27. Prophecy that does not lead to him is a map with no destination.
The timeline that predicted Christ's first advent to bear our sins guarantees his second
advent to reign as king. Rest in that triumph, not in fear of present superpowers.
